lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach the woody halophyte branch of Caryophyllales using scale leaves, racemes and tufted seeds.

project_scope.note: Both current project taxa, Tamarix aphylla and T. ramosissima, are introduced in Texas according to current Kew distributions; use as invasive/landscape recognition, not native anchors.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with the woody branchlets carrying minute scale-like leaves, then confirm many small 4–5-part flowers in racemes/spikes and a dry capsule containing numerous tiny seeds with apical hair tufts.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Xerophytic or halophytic shrubs and small trees with slender branchlets and very small alternate scale- or awl-like leaves, often glandular.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers small, radial and bisexual, commonly 4- or 5-merous in racemes or spikes. Petals and sepals are distinct; stamens are commonly as many as the petals or twice as many and associated with a disk.
family_diagnostics.fruit: A capsule with numerous tiny seeds; seeds often carry an apical tuft of hairs aiding wind dispersal.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Scale-leaved woody plant + pink/white racemes + tufted tiny seeds is the Tamaricaceae package.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: scale leaves → raceme → 5-part flower → capsule → tufted seed → nonnative status
visual_lesson.intro: Tamaricaceae looks conifer-like vegetatively but reveals itself as an angiosperm the moment you inspect the racemes and tufted seeds.

steps.title: 1 · Start with the scale-like leaves
steps.look_for: Minute appressed or sheath-like leaves on slender green/reddish branchlets.
steps.why_it_matters: This creates the false-conifer gestalt the crew is likely to notice first.

steps.title: 2 · Find the flower racemes
steps.look_for: Dense racemes or spikes of many tiny 4–5-part flowers.
steps.why_it_matters: The flowers immediately show this is not a conifer.

steps.title: 3 · Open the capsule and find the hair tuft
steps.look_for: Numerous tiny seeds, each with an apical tuft of hairs.
steps.why_it_matters: The seed tuft is a memorable family confirmation and dispersal clue.

steps.title: 4 · Flag the project status
steps.photo_role: T. aphylla vs T. ramosissima comparison
steps.look_for: Both are introduced Texas taxa in current Kew distribution data.
steps.why_it_matters: Keeps crew recognition separate from native-plant endorsement.

comparisons.title: Tamaricaceae vs Cupressaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can look scale-leaved. Tamarix has true flowers in racemes and capsules with tufted seeds; junipers/cypresses have cones and no flowers.

comparisons.title: Tamaricaceae vs Plumbaginaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can tolerate saline/arid settings, but Tamaricaceae is woody and scale-leaved with racemes and many tufted seeds; Plumbaginaceae uses a persistent tubular calyx and one-seeded fruit.

visual_lesson.caveat: The two project Tamarix species are introduced comparisons. Family recognition is useful for management and invasive-plant ID, not native restoration selection.

genera.fast_cue: woody scale-leaved branchlets + dense tiny flower racemes + tufted seeds
